questions.question: What defining property identifies the zero vector $\boldsymbol0$?
options: $\boldsymbol0$ is any scalar equal to zero.

questions.question: Why is the zero vector called an additive identity?
options: It changes each vector into its inverse.
Adding it leaves every vector unchanged.
Multiplying by it leaves every scalar unchanged.
It is the only vector with no coordinates in $\mathbb{R}^n$.

questions.question: In $\mathbb{R}^n$, what is the zero vector?
options: Any vector whose coordinates sum to $0$.

questions.question: Is the zero vector unique in a vector space?
options: Only if the vector space has a basis.
Only in $\mathbb{R}^2$, not in other spaces.
Yes, there is only one additive identity.
No, every vector can be a zero vector.

Why is the scalar $0$ not literally the same object as the zero vector in $\mathbb{R}^2$?
options: They are the same object in every vector space, written with the same symbol $0$ in both roles.
The scalar has two coordinates and the vector has none.
The zero vector is not used in vector spaces.
The scalar is a field element, while the zero vector is $(0,0)$ in the vector space.

questions.question: If two vectors both behave as additive identities, what must be true?
Why must every vector space contain a zero vector?
options: Because closure under addition alone forces it to exist.
Because $x+(-x)$ must give the scalar $0$ for every $x$.
Because an additive identity is one of the axioms.
Because every vector space is some $\mathbb{R}^n$ with an origin.

questions.question: Which equation shows that $(0,0,0)$ is the zero vector for $(a,b,c)$?
What is $5\boldsymbol0$ in any vector space?
options: A vector different from $\boldsymbol0$ in general.
Undefined, since zero cannot be scaled.

questions.question: What vector must be added to $(1,-4)$ to get the zero vector?
Why is $0v=\boldsymbol0$ not merely a notation convention?
options: It says every vector equals zero.
It is false in most vector spaces and is only adopted as a convention.
It is a theorem following from the vector-space rules.
It means the scalar $0$ is a vector.

questions.question: What would go wrong if a space had two different additive identities?
options: The identity element would not be unique, contradicting a basic vector-space result.
The dimension of the space would become infinite, since each identity adds a new direction.
